old_title: Swinney insists 'stars are aligning' for Scottish independence
new_title: Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at Burnham
old_text:
- Published
John Swinney will insist that "the stars are aligning" for Scottish independence during his keynote speech to the SNP conference later.
The first minister will tell party members in Aberdeen that 2026 has been a turning point in the country's "journey towards statehood".
Swinney will stress that "in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast, every first minister now supports our nations' right to self-determination".
He will seek to press the case for another independence referendum in the wake of elections in May which saw the SNP win a record fifth term in government at Holyrood.
The nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland held a summit in Cardiff last month where they signed an agreement, which is not legally binding, that said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".
Swinney will tell his party's supporters that "one by one, the stars are aligning in our favour".
He will say that if the SNP lost May's Scottish Parliament election, the case for independence "would have been set back decades".
While the SNP won the Holyrood ballot, the party failed to win the overall majority Swinney had set as a target for trying to force a second referendum in the face of Westminster opposition.
Despite that, Swinney will declare that "there is no turning back".
He is expected to say: "The SNP is making the weather.
"And make no mistake â the wind is now firmly in the sails of Scotland's independence movement."
The first minister will go on to claim that the unionist parties at Westminster are "weaker than they have ever been".
Swinney's address to the SNP conference comes the day after Andy Burnham made his first major speech in Scotland since moving into Downing Street.
The prime minister used that visit to extend an olive branch to Swinney, saying he wanted to work together on giving more power to local communities.
Speaking in Motherwell, the Labour leader said he wanted to "move beyond the old politics of conflict" as he offered to work with the SNP to deepen devolution in Scotland.
Burnham previously told Swinney during a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".
The meeting came after Burnham told MPs that a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.
Since 2014, successive UK governments have opposed any further referendums.
Scotland previously voted against becoming an independent country by 55% to 45%.
In 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled that any further vote would require the agreement of the UK government.
new_text:
- Published
John Swinney has taken aim at those who think Scotland "should be just like Manchester" as he vowed Scotland would soon be an independent nation.
In a closing speech at the SNP conference that did not mention Prime Minister Andy Burnham by name, Swinney issued a veiled retort to the former Greater Manchester mayor after he visited Scotland.
The first minister, speaking in Aberdeen, also announced that the country's bus network would be brought under public control by the end of the parliamentary term in 2031.
Swinney made further pledges to extend a Â£2 bus fare cap to the north east of Scotland, launch an independence campaign, fund anti-racism initiatives and tackle misogyny in schools.
Swinney began and ended his speech by talking about the constitution, saying that "the stars are aligning" for supporters of Scottish independence.
He pointed to the SNP's election victory in May. The result delivered a record number of pro-independence MSPs at Holyrood - though the proportion of pro-independence votes decreased from about 50% in 2021 to about 41% this year.
The Scottish government is hoping to hold a second referendum by 2031.
Burnham, who would need to agree to a vote, has told Swinney such a move was "off limits".
Taking aim at the Labour leader, the first minister said: "Some think we should just be like Manchester. Well I'm afraid I disagree
"Scotland is no city. We are no region. We are a nation
"And soon we will be an independent nation."
SNP 'war chest'
Swinney cited the signing of a non-binding agreement between the nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland last month vowing that no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".
He also said the SNP would launch its "most sophisticated" independence campaign yet, backed by the party's "six-figure war chest".
The SNP leader said the campaign, called Choose Scotland, is to include a national day of action, digital and broadcast adverts, and an independence survey delivered to almost 1.5m people.
Swinney told party members it would offer hope and ambition and that independence would deliver "the best possible future" for Scots.
Ending his speech, the SNP leader told the audience that his youngest son Matthew served as his inspiration to make Scotland "future fit for our children".
Swinney's address to the SNP conference came the day after Burnham made his first major speech in Scotland since moving into Downing Street.
The prime minister insisted he wanted to work together on giving more power to local communities.
Speaking in Motherwell, the Labour leader said he wanted to "move beyond the old politics of conflict" as he offered to work with the SNP to deepen devolution in Scotland.
Burnham told MPs earlier this year that referendums would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.
However, he told Swinney at a subsequent meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remained "off limits".
Scotland voted against becoming an independent country by 55% to 45% in 2014.
In 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled that any further vote would require the agreement of the UK government - something successive prime ministers have refused to countenance.
Earlier in his speech, Swinney announced that a Â£2 bus fare cap would be extended to the north east of Scotland from April.
Swinney told SNP members that "cheaper bus travel is only one part of the story".
"We need more buses and we need more frequent buses," he said. "It's good for commuters. And it's good for the climate.
"I can therefore announce today that by the end of this parliament, through franchising and regulation, the SNP will bring the bus network back into public control."
Bus fares are currently capped at Â£2 in the west of Scotland and the Highlands, with a national rollout promised by 2031.
Bus operators are given government subsidies to participate.
Swinney also announced a Â£30m fund for community groups to help "combat the rise of the racists", and a new bill to make harassment and abuse based on misogyny a specific criminal offence.
He added that the government would launch a Â£1m "respect fund giving every school the resources they need to tackle misogyny".
